chapter_title: The Chapter of the Nazorean who questions the Teacher
chapter_note: This chapter is overwhelmingly a later dialogical apologetic/pastoral unit: a framed encounter (Nazorean vs. the apostle) built around a moral-judicial analogy (God as judge) and ethical recompense. It lacks the impersonal, systematic cosmos→cosmos correspondential mappings that mark the oldest substrate. One paragraph (¶10) explicitly enters via a Gospel saying (Mt 6), making it Christian overlay. The remaining discourse is exhortative/moral reasoning about sin, punishment, reward, and the devil—application to moral life rather than cosmological architecture.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Formulaic narrative opening (“Once again, it happened one time…”) and hagiographic/dialogue staging (“Nazorean… before the apostle”)—editorial frame rather than cosmological teaching.
Dialogue attribution (“The apostle speaks…”) plus rhetorical bargaining about ‘one word’ vs ‘many words’; this is scene-setting rhetoric, not impersonal cosmological exposition.
Continuation of the staged disputation; question posed within the dialogue frame, with no systematic cosmological content.

Strong dialogue apparatus (“Then says the apostle… Then the apostle says…”) and polemical quip. The line “A [ju]dge is my God” is presented as part of the editorialized encounter, not a substrate mapping within the cosmic system.

Narrated opponent speech expanding the courtroom analogy (lashes, racks, chains, sword). This is argumentative dialogue content embedded in the hagiographic disputation scene, not the correspondential substrate.

Moral-theological reasoning (judge limits evil; punishment falls on the sinner). Even though introduced by “The apostle… speaks,” the content is not a cosmos→cosmos structure but ethical/apologetic discourse—typical pastoral/application teaching.
Direct exhortation/application voice (“pay attention to this”) and ethical reassurance about the innocent before the judge; this is applied moral instruction, not substrate cosmology.
Ethical causality (“he brings his sin… upon his own head”) and recompense for good deeds. The logic is moral-judicial application rather than impersonal cosmic mechanics.

Explicit application to God as judge of souls, with moral dualism framed in behavioral terms (“obey the devil… be won over to the truth”). This remains application discourse, not systematic cosmological correspondence.

Christian overlay signaled by citation formula and Gospel-derived saying: “Even as the saviour has said: Where your heart is, your treasure…” (Mt 6). Entered the Kephalaia via NT tradition regardless of its moral-causal argument.
Moral retribution language (deeds condemn; gehenna of burning). This is ethical-eschatological warning, not the older impersonal cosmological mapping layer.

Ethical recompense and reward (“good deeds… kingdom of light… life eternal”). ‘Kingdom of light’ vocabulary is used devotionally/eschatologically here rather than as a structured cosmological degree-map.
Concluding exhortative summation (“Behold now… you see…”), reiterating the judge analogy. Closure is didactic/application rather than substrate exposition.
